claims.text: The investigated AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are smaller than 5 nm.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
The nanoparticles possess a metastable FCC structure stabilized by kinetic effects rather than thermodynamic entropy.
In bulk high-entropy alloys, sluggish diffusion can inhibit atomic transport.
Surface-energy contributions dominate the bulk configurational-entropy contribution in AuCoCuNiPt particles below 10 nm.
Atomic-radius mismatch between Au/Cu and Pt/Ni contributes to a chemical-potential gradient.
Au and Cu are the low-melting-point species relevant to segregation in this quinary nanoparticle system.
Differences in melting behavior can be associated with elemental segregation.
A thermodynamic driving force can produce elemental phase separation in a multicomponent alloy.
The high surface-to-volume ratio creates a steep chemical-potential gradient that drives rapid outward diffusion in sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Au and Cu segregate to the nanoparticle surface to reduce surface energy.
Surface diffusion faces lower long-range transport barriers than bulk diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Au/Cu surface segregation creates a volatile-rich surface layer that subsequently evaporates.
Evaporation of the segregated surface layer causes particle mass loss and widening of the particle-size distribution.
The depleted particle core becomes spherical to minimize its surface area.
For sub-5 nm particles, a critical temperature of approximately 500–600 K marks the point where Au/Cu segregation and evaporation become dominant over bulk diffusion.
The FCC structure is lost through depletion of stabilizing elements rather than through a polymorphic phase transition.
The proposed surface-energy-dominated mechanism is restricted to particles below 10 nm and does not apply to bulk HEAs.
